The traditional understanding of Digital Manufacturing describes the utilization of a suite of tools to facilitate the integration of product and process design.
The concept of Digital Manufacturing has evolved from a focus on cost-driven manufacturing to a more knowledge-based approach.
The absence of physical tooling in Additive Manufacturing (AM) carries the advantage of being able to deposit complex product geometries without many constraints.
AM allows for the efficient manufacture of very small quantities of products, down to a single unit.
Data science techniques, including machine learning, have been used in automated manufacturing for predictive maintenance, demand forecasting, process monitoring, and optimization.
The key challenge faced by industry is to find expertise in both the areas of data science and optimization, as each poses its own problems and requires an inherently different skill set.
The integrated framework for Digital Manufacturing describes the conceptual basis for the development of integrated approaches to problems, such as scheduling and packing.
The evolved understanding of Digital Manufacturing places a greater emphasis on flexibility, reconfigurability, and resilience in the operation of manufacturing systems.
The data infrastructure provided by the integrated framework of Digital Manufacturing gives rise to new opportunities for the concurrent application of data science and optimization techniques.

The integrated framework for assessing Digital Manufacturing combines a Digital Manufacturing model, a generic Additive Manufacturing process map, and a life cycle assessment framework.
